utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you call the case, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Wednesday, 26 of September 2007, I would like to greet everyone in this courtroom; Mr. Scott, on behalf of the Prosecution; the witness; all of the members of the Defence teams; in particular, Mr. Murphy, who will not be with us for much longer. So I'd like to extend him a particularly warm welcome; and, of course, my greetings to the accused as well; and all of those who help us to fulfil our mission. Now it is time for the re-examination. We have time for us,, exceptionally, and I give the floor to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom. And, good morning, Dr. Miller.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't hear. Obviously, I can understand, but something is not on. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can just -- if I could ask the usher's assistance, we might as well do it now, if we could bring up all of the exhibits, please, and if the witness could be supplied the exhibits, please. Might as well give him - we won't use all - but the easiest thing to do is to give them all to him. Perhaps, I'm sorry, it's the third binder, I think. It's the smaller of the third binder is, probably, the one that may be needed. Thank you. Thank you, Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, I'd like to cover a few topics that were raised during your cross-examination. The first of those is on the topic of separate armies in the federation, which you were asked about on several occasions, in particular by Mr. Karnavas. In particular, Mr. Karnavas asked you about a statement that was made on page 2 of your, what I'll call the, Herceg-Bosna Report, P10240. You have that in front of you. Just refresh everyone's memory. In the bottom of the main text on page 2 of that report, I'll just pause to make sure everyone has had a chance to find that. Toward the bottom of that page, of the main text, you say, this was the statement where you attributed -- you quoted material attributed to Mr. Prce saying: "the Croat side does not support a unified army in BiH." You recall both that statement and the questions that you were asked during cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that I was asked questions. I don't think I recall them specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You discussed, let me put it then in this further context, you discussed with Mr. Karnavas that at that time, in the two entity arrangement, that is, the BiH Federation, the Croats and Muslims, on the one hand, and the Serb entity, the Republika Srpska, on the other, there were armies or were supposed to be armies at the entity level; that is, what was -- in terms of the Federation, there was supposed to be a federation army. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in writing, what you wrote here, again, by way of reference, since Mr. Karnavas questioned you about that, if you look in your report, it actually goes over to the top of page 3 until we get to footnote 7, you will see that what was referenced, what you cited or quoted from was something called, "Is Dayton Failing," which, obviously as we can all see, was part of your report, although that particular document was not previously marked as an individual exhibit. In light of the questions that were raised, I've now had that marked as Exhibit P10286, which I believe has been put in front of you and was distributed this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I know it went to Defence counsel. I assume the Chamber has it as well. It's P10286. It's a longer document but there is only a couple of small parts or one small part that I direct your attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The material you quoted from, and in light of the discussion that you had with Mr. Karnavas, let me ask you to go to page -- the numbers are -- excuse me, the pages are numbered on the top right corner, and if you can go to page 8 of the document, you'll see that, if you go to the bottom of page 8 E, the Federation army HVO and ABiH, I'm putting that in context; then if you go to the top of page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the top of page 9, again just to put it in context, the carry over from the previous page says, "Rather, party loyalty has become the primary criteria for command in the Federation army." Then, what you quoted from in your report comes next, when it says, "The reasons for this was explained by the Federation Defence Minister, Miroslav Prce: 'The Croat side does not support a unified army in BiH because we do not want to create another mini former JNA,'" which then continues on as the same quote. That is on page 2 of your report that I directed your attention to a moment ago. Now, sir, my question to you is: Is it correct that the statement attributed to Mr. Prce and the discussion that is it being had here is specifically in the context of the Federation army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is improper redirect examination because he's talking about an army for BiH. There is nothing here about a Federation or an entity. We are talking about one particular army, and he quoted. The quote is here. It's up to the Trial Chamber now to determine. This gentleman did not create the report. He did not interview the gentleman who made the report. The Trial Chamber can read the quote and can determine whether it's to the Federation or to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina altogether, but he is not qualified at this point to give some sort of a guess or an assumption as to what exactly the gentleman meant. It is, the text speaks for itself. That's the best evidence that we have. Not what this person thinks the individual meant at the time, because it's very clear what army they are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, so says Mr. Karnavas. So says, so argues Mr. Karnavas, but that's not -- you're exactly right, the document speaks for itself, and what Mr. Karnavas didn't point out to the Chamber and when the Chamber did not have the full document in front of it. As it does now, you can plainly see that the entire context of the discussion is the Federation army. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is not my --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Beyond that, I, indeed, leave it to the Chamber to properly draw its conclusion, but it was this man who cited it in his report; and contrary to what Mr. Karnavas says, it is this man who knows the proposition for which he cited it, not Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just point out for the record that, when the Prosecution brings in a witness and does a direct examination, it is for the Prosecution to provide the Trial Chamber with all the information. I'm working off of what they provided me. I'm working off the direct examination. To now try to play the victim, that somehow the Prosecution has been victimised by this bad old Karnavas is simply wrong. It's pure bad advocacy on the part of the Prosecution. He could have simply pointed this out with the gentleman on direct examination, but to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No need to, Your Honour, until Mr. Karnavas took the matter of the material out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I took it the way it was presented in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we are wasting time, once again. The Judges will have to rule in the long run on your thesis, on your submissions, and those of the Prosecution. We have before us a document that is relevant, since it is directly related to your cross-examination, page 8, paragraph E: The armies of the Federation, HVO, ABiH. So we are really completely within the topic. So, between what the witness says and the document says, the Judges will be able to assess the issue. So let Mr. Scott ask the questions, the witness will answer, and then we shall see. So please pursue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That actually concludes on that particular document, but leading then to the three documents, the three signed documents, if you will, then, part of Exhibit P10267, that were discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can go to that, Dr. Miller, I believe it will be in that smaller of the third binder, 10267, which a number of people have spoken to you about. For reasons discussed yesterday, I'm skipping past the first 18 pages; and if you could please go to the document within that larger document, that is a letter or report, excuse me, a report dated the 29th of June 1998, from a Lieutenant General Stanko Sopta to Ante Jelavic, the Minister of Defence. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Miller, I'm putting these documents and these questions to you in the context of the question of the separation of the two armies that you talk about in that part of your and other parts of your second report, and I would just like you to look -- I would just like to point you to several parts of the document and then ask you a couple of questions. In the first paragraph of that document, although the paragraphs might not be entirely clear, but there is a paragraph -- there is a sentence that says, "Under such conditions," and then it goes on to say, at the ends of that, it says, "to build up a military power system that will serve as a guarantee of the existence of the Croatian people in BiH." And, then, in section 1, it talks about schooling, and the context will indicate we are talking about military training, academy, training, in the Republic of Croatia. Going on to the first paragraph, starting on the second page, it refers to military schools in the Republic of Croatia should be the basis. In approximately the middle of that page, in the middle of the paragraph, in the middle of that page, it talks about, "complete orientation toward the Republic of Croatia, compatibility with commanding personnel in the arm forces of the Republic of Croatia, which is necessary in cases of synchronised activity." If you go to page 3 of the document, the first so-called bullet item on that page, the status of HVO members, "to be solved by official recognition of the entire time period of every member of military personnel who participate in the home land war, and by making a payment for pension and medical insurance benefits in the Republic of Croatia for the entire period." The next bullet item, "to level the status of HVO members with the status," with the status, "of HV, army of Croatia, members, the regular payments of salaries and all social and retirement benefits." Next page, it references to financial issues, giving numbers in kuna per month. The Chamber will recall, by now, that "kuna" was the Croatian currency at this time; not the currency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the currency of the Republic of Croatia. Further down on that page, in the next to the last paragraph, again, it talks about the Croatian population in BiH, and in the last line, "will defend Croatian territory and interests in BiH." And in the last two pages, 5 and 6, it discusses the building of barracks for this HVO army, even without SFOR, UNPROFOR, the international peacekeeping force had by 1998 become SFOR; and, in the middle of page 5, it talks about, "in order to overcome the situation, we propose to start with building the barracks in private arrangements, which means without approval of the SFOR. And, then, on the bottom of page 6, carrying over to page -- excuse me, page 5 carrying over to page 6, it talks about how this can be done; and even if SFOR turns out to prohibit it, it can be left -- it can be still be set aside and used later or when SFOR leaves, at the top of page 6. Sir, with all that in mind, can you tell the junction whether that information would be consistent with what you found in researching your second report about the desire to maintain the HVO as a separate military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that the implication from this letter goes beyond even that and suggests that the HVO, or at least this person, would have liked the HVO to become, in essence, a part of the army of the Republic of Croatia; so, yes, and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to go to that part of that longer, larger document, again, which is a letter dated the 26th or a report dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, since we are on this document now, I'm wondering who actually wrote this document. So was it written by someone who was very close to the Republic of Croatia or someone from the outside, someone who was neutral, and so on and so forth? It's obvious that, for a historian, the author of a document can -- is very relevant to the meaning of the document, depending on the ideas and mental patterns of the author, as well as the author's aspirations. When you studied this document, did you analyse those criteria? You see that the document says certain things. Did you ask yourself who is the author, what was his purpose, what was the context, why did he write this document? Did you ask yourself that type of question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I looked at the document, I looked at the first 18 pages most closely, and I do not know any of the biographical details about Stanko Sopta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you studied the content without asking yourself any questions regarding the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then pursue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might just assist the Chamber, and I'm sure the Chamber has seen this, but this is a report from Mr. Sopta, who is indicated as Lieutenant-General and the commander of the 1st Croatian Guards Corps; and on the front page of the report, the letterhead, if you will, indicates Joint Command of the Federation, 1st Croatian Guards Corps of the Federation Army to Minister of Defence Ante Jelavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you, Dr. Miller, then, to find the next document, which is, I believe, a report from this same Mr. Jelavic to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, dated the 26th of June 1998. Let me know, please, when you have that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just again point out a couple of -- several things, only a few things in this letter, and you will see, again, on the first page, the second part of the page starts with, "We drew up an estimation of financial means in kunas," which, as we saw a moments ago, is the currency of the Republic of Croatia. And, then, in that regard, if I can ask you to look to about the middle of the second page, where it gives the financial needs for the first half of 1998, I would like to use -- there is different numbers here, so we can just use one number, one currency as a point of reference. I'm going to talk about kuna. Do you agree that it appears to indicate that, for the first half of 1998, the HVO would be founded approximately 50 million kuna from the Federation of BiH; and, during the same period of time, it would be funded by 80 million kuna per month, it should be said, per month, from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, actually, the HVO is receiving more money from the Republic of Croatia to support itself in its operation than it was receiving from the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the last document, very briefly, is a one-page report -- well, one page with attachments, excuse me, dated the 4th of June 1998, again, within the HVO from someone who is listed as the assistant to the Minister and then Miroslav Prce, and indicating various financial needs for, again, the HVO in the June 1998 time frame. Do you see that the number indicated is 342 million, again, Croatian kuna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, once again, Dr. Miller, those additional two documents that I've just taken you to, how do those fit into your report, the parts of your report, your second report, where you talk about the maintenance of a second or separate HVO army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first of these two additional documents, you know, we can draw from this that the HVO was reliant on the Republic of Croatia for funding --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- which I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead, please, if you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we are extrapolating, but the first of these two documents, the fact that the Republic of Croatia is paying approximately 45 per cent more - I don't know quick math - than the federation itself, yeah, it would imply that the HVO is reliant or perhaps over-reliant on the Republic of Croatia for funding. I guess that it would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving from that topic to a couple of miscellaneous, I might call them miscellaneous, questions before we come back to one or two of the major topics that were put to you during cross-examination. Mr. Karnavas also asked you about what services were being provided by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and, by that, I guess it is typically meant that these purposes the government in Sarajevo, in the time period around, and I'm not sure it was exactly specified, but 1992, 1993. I believe your testimony or your answer in response to Mr. Karnavas, What services were being provided at least in some areas, I think you said, "Probably none." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me just try to clarify your answer a little bit. How about Defence? Was the government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina providing Defence and fighting the Serbs, for example, in Eastern Bosnia and the Croats in various parts of Bosnian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. First of all, he said, "Probably yes," meaning that -- or, "Probably none," whatever the answer was on cross-examination. In other words, it was speculative at best. First, does he have actual knowledge? Did he study? Let's lay a foundation; otherwise, we are just asking him to speculate based on -- or leading him down the road, asking leading questions where he's going to say, Yes, of course. Perhaps the gentleman would be asked, then, What sort of financial assistance or military assistance the Muslim government was getting from Croatia and from Iran and from Saudi Arabia and from Afghanistan and all the Mujahedin? We can go down the road. He either knows or he doesn't know. If he doesn't know on cross, he certainly doesn't know on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting, Your Honour, because Mr. Karnavas had no objections to the witness's answers during cross-examination, when the witness said, "Probably none," and I didn't hear Mr. Karnavas withdraw his question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- or the answer, because he says now that the witness was speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because at that point, there is no need to go on. Once he says, "Probably none," am I to press him some more? Because he's demonstrating that he doesn't have knowledge on that. Now, if he wants to lay a foundation and proceed, I don't have a problem, but let's lay a foundation and let's ask non-leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is entirely appropriate reply to questions put by Mr. Karnavas in his cross-examination. It's entirely appropriate that the witness be allowed to clarify an answer that he gave during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I have a ruling, please, Your Honours? May I have a ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Mr. Karnavas wants to know whether or not the witness has actual knowledge with regard to the questions that you are asking, so I will address him the question. You have heard what the Defence counsel has just said. Do you feel that you are able to answer the question asked to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question asked, in my view, the question asked by the Prosecution is a refinement of the question that Mr. Karnavas asked, when he asked me about services. I took that to mean -- actually, I did not put that in a military context; perhaps, I should. I have -- I have no personal information to impart about the military activities of the Bosnian government during the war. I was not there; however, the common sense answer, the common knowledge answer to that question is, yes, the Bosnian government did provide military services to others in Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether the government in Sarajevo facilitated and provided for the delivery in various places of humanitarian aid, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I have no specific knowledge. I couldn't say chapter and verse, but I think it's general knowledge that that's the case, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was health care, education, pension funds, salaries. That is what we are talking about. The electricity, water, what were their capabilities? That was the nature of the question. We are not talking about whether they were funding their own military or providing humanitarian assistance that was coming in to their own people. That's not the essence. We are talking about at the state level, the state institutions. What were the responsibilities towards its people, the Bosnia-Herzegovinians, whether they be Croat, Muslim or Serb, and what was it able to provide at the time. That was the essence. Now, if the gentleman knows, concretely, fine; otherwise, these are self-serving questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Karnavas, who is raising the question, has already raised the question with other witnesses; and, hence, it's obviously a question that's important to him. The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina presided by Izetbegovic, well, was the government able to meet the obligations of any government with regard to education, pensions, salaries, water, electricity, and so on and so forth, everything that you see on line 13 and 14 -- 12 and 13 of page 14. This question has already been raised in this courtroom. To your knowledge, according to your research, having studied reports and articles in the press and the knowledge that you have, did you think about this question or did you not think about this question at all? This is what the Defence would like to know, and the Judges would find it interesting as well. So what do you have to say on that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Categories Mr. Karnavas uses in lines 12 and 13, I did not look at. They were before the scope of the report I was writing and so I did not, and I have no previous outside knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, just to be fair on this, because given what's been said and the questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He cannot pursue --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, He cannot pursue that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, could I be heard one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- to be fair --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- yes, I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- he cannot pursue that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- he can just move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Each one should speak in turn. Mr. Miller, you said that you were not aware of the problems the government might have -- the government headed by Mr. Izetbegovic might have met. You said, "I was not aware of that." Is that what you said? Right. Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Scott got up at the same time. Mr. Karnavas, what did you want to say following this answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to say is the following, Your Honour: Now that we know that he had no prior knowledge, he hasn't studied, there is no foundation, now is the time for Mr. Scott to move on to another question, not to be fair to the gentleman. The gentleman is being treated fairly. He wasn't asked to go into that area, fine. He has no knowledge about that area, fine. But now there is no sense in beating a dead horse. He has to move on. The gentleman does not have the requisite foundational knowledge in order to answer any questions that Mr. Scott wishes to pose. And in fairness to the gentleman, he wasn't asked, one, to determine what were the services that the government had to provide; two, what was it able to provide; three, what did it actually provide? Those were not part -- it's not part of the report. It's not part of the gentleman's knowledge, and so why now is Mr. Scott pursuing the same course of action? He doesn't need to try to rehabilitate the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now let me respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I will be giving you the floor in minutes, as the President. But from what I understand from the discussions, Mr. Karnavas is saying that the witness cannot answer these points because he was not aware of that. And Mr. Karnavas is inviting you to move on to another question because, since he cannot answer, it would be useless to go on in this direction. So you may have a different opinion. What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, you've now allowed Mr. Karnavas to go on several times repeatedly without allowing me to have any time for a response, and I object to that. Now, given the time to respond, it is entirely appropriate on cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, don't say that. I'm just giving you the floor right now to answer, so please answer. Would you like to be mentioned in the transcript that I did not allow you to speak? That's not true, because I just allowed you to take the floor, so don't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You did finally. My point is this: It is entirely appropriate, when the witness is challenged and his credibility is attacked, his report is attacked on a point; and Mr. Karnavas asks him a question and accepts the answer that presumably suits him when he says, when the witness's answer yesterday was, "Probably none," which there was no objection - Mr. Karnavas didn't say there was no basis for the witness's answer; he accepted an answer that he presumed that he liked - it's entirely appropriate on redirect to come back and seek to clarify the witness's answer. If the witness had no information on these matters, then he has no information on this point for either the Prosecution or the Defence. So when he said yesterday, "Probably none," then the answer is to be stricken for all accounts. It didn't support Mr. Karnavas's view and it may not support my view. But what we are seeing here, again, is what sow often happens, Mr. Karnavas wants to play by one sets of rules and he wants the Prosecution to play by a different set of rules. He stands up; and by becoming theatrical, raising his voice with the Court, and waving his arms, he wants to bully the Court to taking a certain position. That is entirely inappropriate. This witness has been treated quite harshly in the last two and a half days, and I simply would like him to give the opportunity to clarify some certain points that were put to him. That's entirely appropriate for redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There were several questions that I was posing to the gentleman, and the answers were, "I don't know," "I don't know," "I don't know." At some point, on more than one occasion, Mr. Scott got up and objected that the gentleman was being treated unfairly and that he was being embarrassed and this was deliberate. Those were questions that were relevant, in my opinion, to the study. So, if he says -- at some point, I was invited by the Trial Chamber to just ask one global question, because it didn't make sense to go into say, -- well, I asked him what was the budget, what was this, what was that, the answer was, "I don't know," "I don't know," "I don't know." So I don't know what the Prosecutor is now claiming. Once the gentleman says that he doesn't -- if he gives me a speculative answer, there is no need for me to press. I accept it. I accept it for what it is; that is, that he's speculating and it has no evidentiary value. So for me to press him at that point doesn't make any sense. All I'm saying is, at this point in time, the gentleman himself has indicated that he doesn't have any knowledge. He wasn't asked to look into it. He wasn't over there during the war period, and he cannot simply ask -- in any question any answers now would be speculative at best. That's why I'm inviting the Trial Chamber to instruct the Prosecution to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, one final comment, one final comment, and then I ask the Court to allow me to ask two more questions on this topic, and I will move on, but one further comment on that. I did object. The Chamber will recall I objected over and over and over again to the -- questions were being put to the witness that were outside the scope of his report and, clearly, for the purposes of embarrassing him, and saying, What do you know about this? How many pension funds existed in Bosnia in 1996? I mean, ridiculous questions this witness couldn't possibly be expected to know off his head. It was badgering the witness. I objected, I objected, I objected, again. The Chamber didn't do anything to stop it. Now, for Mr. Karnavas then to get up and complain plain that and say I'm the one trying to take advantage of the situation is completely wrong. Now, I'd ask the Chamber if I can ask two questions about the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, now you will be able to ask questions, but, Mr. Scott, I don't agree with what you're saying on line 5, page 19. You said that Mr. Karnavas asked questions -- ridiculous questions on pension funds and salaries. No. They are not ridiculous because these are administrative questions related to the budget, and they are included, they are mentioned, in the document. And, since they are mentioned in the document, he is asking questions based on the document. So don't tell me that he's asking ridiculous questions. They may not be relevant. They may not have any probative value. I mean, the answer to the questions may not have a probative value, but the Defence is allowed to ask this type of questions. You may believe that they are ridiculous. They might be ridiculous, but Mr. Karnavas has the right to ask questions. And the witness to say, "I don't know," "I don't know," "I don't know." This is true, and you're 100 per cent right in saying that the witness answered he did not know and you objected because you thought that this was beyond the scope of the study, but the Chamber allowed it to go on because if we decide to simply stick to the scope, the risk is to forget the context and all the background. Sometimes you have to go beyond the scope to understand what is the background and the context. That's all. So the Chamber does not forbid you from asking questions. On the contrary, all we are expecting is just questions, but we would like the questions to be useful and necessary and help us understand this case better. So now you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have two questions on this topic before I move on to another topic, and I didn't really intend for this to be -- go this long. I just want to assure the Chamber. But in light of the various interventions, it's gone longer than I expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, let me just ask you two final questions on this topic, the services and the status and abilities of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina during this periods of time. Did, for example, did the Bosnian government or the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina have an ambassador at the United Nations and representatives who dealt with the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in terms of the questions that were put to you about its ability to deliver social services, for example, to its various citizens, be they Muslim, Croat, or Serb, can you tell the Chamber, please, what do you think would be the impact on Bosnian government's ability to provide such services, for example, in Mostar, where one major party - and I'm not talking about the Serbs - was withdrawing its ministers and representatives from that government, was occupying its sovereign territory, putting its cities and towns under siege, and shooting at and killing his soldiers and representatives?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm going to intervene on this one, because this is this an outrageous question. It's leading. It calls for speculation, and it's quite, obviously, outside the expertise of this witness based on his own testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he's been questioned on why, again, he puts in cross-examination, Why was the government not fulfilling its duties and responsibilities to provide social services? Well, I think it's relevant for the Chamber to know, you know, how were they supposed to do so under the circumstances, when there was, for instance, a city of Mostar that was under siege? They just act like that's somehow not a factor. I think the witness can comment on that, just as he has been allowed to comments on numerous other questions that have been put to him by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are all questions which are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, an intervention on my part. As we are talking about redirect here, it refers to the cross-examination. In the cross examination, clear questions were posed related to 1994 and 1995; and, in most of those questions, that period of time is incorporated. So what services did the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina fulfil in 1994 and 1995? Now, why would we take these years 1994 and 1995? Because the entire report refers to the period after the Washington Agreement. So that is the basic subject of the entire cross-examination that was conducted. Why did Herceg-Bosna continue to function after the Washington agreement? That is why the questions were asked. What powers did the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina have? This is directly related to the report, where it says quite clearly, "Social and other services are handed via Herceg-Bosna rather than through the BH government." That's what it says, and that was the foundation, that was the basis, upon which my Defence counsel asked all his questions. Who was in charge of supplying electricity? Who paid out the pensions? Who was in charge of providing water, the water supply? Was there a Bosnia-Herzegovinian budget in 1994, yes or no? So those were the questions that my Defence counsel asked, and the Prosecution in redirect absolutely does have the right to deal with those questions, if it considers that the witness did not provide the answers that he deemed should have been given. But now he's dealing with questions that were not raised in the cross-examination. So the questions weren't related to the situation of war but the subject that we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Mr. Prlic has just made a statement, and he said that redirect questions can be asked when they have a direct connection with the questions raised during the cross-examination. Now, if you start dealing with the "siege of Mostar," in between inverted commas, this is something which has not been mentioned during the cross-examination. This is where the problem lies. You want to deal with something which has not been dealt with before. So, in this case, you have to ask the Chamber for the authorisation to raise this type of question. This is what the rules stipulate, and this is what Mr. Prlic was mentioning since he knows the rules as well as I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate being counseled on points of practice of law by Mr. Prlic. I think my error was in using the siege of Mostar as a particular example, and I would modify my question to that extent. My general point to the witness was what can you expect the kind of services to be provided under wartime conditions, which did indeed continue after 1993 into 1994 into 1995, the very period that was being discussed? But, Your Honour, I think the point has been made; and, in the interests of time, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, another point: At one point, Mr. Karnavas was questioning about value judgements; and, at one point, he did volunteer that he liked your value judgement, apparently, and that's going to be my question. He said that you had expressed a value judgement indicating that Mr. Prlic was a moderate. Now, I want to be clear about this because I, for one, did not hear or see that answer in your testimony, so I want to ask you: Did you testify that you, Dr. Miller, considered Mr. Prlic to be a moderate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. If the Prosecutor would like to quote the text, because the context in which that came in - and I don't mean to be obstreperous; he can answer the question - is where the gentleman indicated, and I believe it's at the bottom of page 1: "Some of the more moderate Bosnian Croats were dispatched to the Federation and the state government," and we all know what positions Dr. Prlic held during that period of time, in post. The gentleman didn't know, didn't know, for instance, that Mr. Prlic was the Minister of Defence for the Federation. He knew that he was the Minister of Foreign Affairs after Dayton, but he didn't know all the others positions that Dr. Prlic held. But if you reed this saying -- if you go on, he's talking about the "hard liners," whoever they may be, stayed behind. And the question had to do with, Who was dispatched -- Who was dispatching those who were being dispatched? And since Dr. Prlic was one of the individuals who was participating heavily in the establishment of the Federation and in posts-Dayton events, I took it upon myself to say, Well, obviously, if he's being dispatched and he's part of the Federation government, he must be included in one of these moderates because of the context. Now, if he wants to rephrase the question, that's fine. But that's the context in which it was raised, and the gentleman could not provide an answer as to who was being the dispatching.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I remember, Your Honour, quite clearly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he can quote the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- that Mr. Karnavas said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- he can quote the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas said something very close to the effect, "I like your value judgement," indicating that Mr. Prlic was a moderate, and I simply would like to make clear, so the record is indeed clear, so it's not mischaracterised some six months or a year from now, as to what the witness's evidence on that and whether he expressed a value judgement, Dr. Miller's value judgement, as whether Mr. Prlic was a moderate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally expressed no judgement as to whether Mr. Prlic is a moderate or something else. The judgement in the report that I used was that moderates collectively were sent to Sarajevo to get them out of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you don't know whether -- you don't have any independent knowledge whether Mr. Prlic was considered one of those moderates or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Turning to the media articles that you talked about, and there was extensive cross-examination from a number of parties on that, your references to, for example, -- what we are getting into now is your references to Danas and Vreme and that part of your second report -- well, no, excuse me, primarily your first report on the patterns and practices in the conflict. If I could just start, if I might be able to assist, you were trying to remember the name of another Croat publication that you said you had referred to. I may be wrong, but might it possibly have been Slobodani Tjednik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. On the first day, on Monday, on the top of page 19 of the first report, Exhibit P10239, top of page 19, I put this to you on Monday just as an essentially a summary statement of the -- at the ends of your report, quoting: "Thus, by mid-1992, a pattern of violence purposely focused on civilians as a means of compelling them to abandon a given territory had emerged and was widely reported and known locally, regionally, and internationally." And my first question to you is: Following the rather intensive cross-examination, Dr. Miller --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can finish my question, if I can at least finish my question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- whether in light of the -- despite the cross-examination that you've been exposed to in the past several days, whether you continue to stand by that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I had an objection to the transcript, but it seems to have become clear in the meantime, so I won't take up any more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see in the answer Dr. Miller that your answer was that you continue to stand behind that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you did your research, is it fair to say that you were conducting your research, not as someone who was a novice or new to the topic of Yugoslavia, but as someone who has spent the last 15 or 20 years, 15 or 20 years, studying, reading about, teaching about, writing about, Yugoslavia and the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I understood the cross-examination, I think one of the points that was being made is that both Vreme and Danas tended to be read by, IF I understood you correctly or the questions that were put to you, among others by more educated people, at least that seemed to be a part of what was being said. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The articles you cited in your papers, when you cited those, was it your idea or intention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you wait a minute, Mr. Scott. Mr. Praljak got up. Mr. Praljak, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How does the witness know that Danas and Vreme was read by educated people? On the basis of what research is he able it to know that and say that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the question put to him by Mr. Petkovic's counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise but my question wasn't put that way at all. I don't know the structure of the readers of either Vreme or Danas. What I did mention was the word "intellectuals" in the context of several people in Sarajevo, a number of people in Sarajevo who probably read Vreme and Danas, and that's the only thing that I said, the only adjective I used. Otherwise, I don't consider that there is any research on the makeup of the readers of journals like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miller, there are two newspapers, Vreme and Danas, read by readers. It seems that there is a discussion on the type of readers. Do the readers -- given the quality of the articles written in these newspapers, are these readers people who have a certain education, or are these newspapers which can be read by just anyone, or is it necessary to have a certain level of education to understand the articles written in these newspapers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One simply has to be able to read, Your Honour. There -- they make no special demands on the reader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. Okay. One just has simply to be able to read, but let me take one typically French example to make you understand what I'm talking about. We have different types of news papers in France, but we have news papers that not everybody can read. Everybody how knows how to read is able to read, but let me make it more diplomatic as an example. The French farmer will not be reading Le Monde Diplomatique. So that's the problem. Concerning these two newspapers we are talking about, do you believe that a farmer in Bosnia and Herzegovina is able to read these newspapers? Being able to read is one thing, but you have to be able to understand what is written in the newspaper. It's just the same as was your thesis. Everybody can read your thesis, but you still need to be able to understand what you're reading. I'm talking about your Ph.D. thesis. Anybody can read it, but you have to be able to understand it. Reading is not understanding, and it is the understanding of the content of the articles that is the issue Ms. Alaburic had mentioned. Do you have an answer to that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, but I'd like to avoid getting into any value judgements about the capabilities of Serbian Muslim or Croatian peasants in Bosnia, and just say Vreme and Danas are news weeklies. I would say that they are no more taxing on the intellect or -- of the given reader than Time or Newsweek in the United States. I don't read French, and I don't have personal experience with the French press. So, I mean, the greater question I suppose is: Who actually does do the reading? But they are not -- they are not particularly taxing journals, magazines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I feel the need to clarify my question. My question about some dozen intellectuals in Sarajevo did not have to do with the quality of the texts contained in the articles contained in Vreme and Danas and the intellectual capabilities for understanding those texts. My question, in fact, referred to the following fact: That throughout the conflict, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, there were a certain number of intellectuals in Sarajevo, Zagreb, and Belgrade, who endeavoured to read all the newspapers from that area, regardless of whether they were printed in Sarajevo, Belgrade, or Zagreb, but that it was a very, very small number of people, mostly people who delved in some intellectual activity. The publications weren't accessible to the population at large. People in rural areas didn't have access to that kind of media and never saw those publications. So that's what I wanted to say in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mrs. Alaburic clarified what she meant in her question. This seems to be clear. Do you have any answer? Mr. Miller, do you have any answer to what Mrs. Alaburic just said, or do you agree with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I can give you a proper answer, I'm going to look at what she said again. In general, I don't disagree with that. I think there is more to be said about the nature of my report in that sense, but I don't disagree with her comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. We have made progress. Mr. Scott, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps, if I have used the word "intellectual" instead of more educated people, we might have avoided some of that. But, be that as it may, my next question to you, sir, before coming back a bit on this topic, would have been -- is this: The articles that you cited in your papers, when you cited those - and I think you indicated this, but, again, because of the extent of cross-examination, I just want to give you a further opportunity to be as clear as possible - was it your idea or intention that when you cited these articles that -- these were the media reports, what have you. I'm saying articles, media items, was it your idea or intention that these are the only items reporting this information, or did you cite these particular papers or items as being representative, albeit you've said they were more moderate, but representative of the local and regional coverage more broadly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I consulted more, and I found this -- I included these because they were representative of broader coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And going back to the question of the circulation of some of these publications, would it be correct to say that just as a say a Bosnian, to use the term that sometimes we have been asked to be very specific, if a Bosnian Croat in Sarajevo or a Herzegovinian Croat in Mostar would today, for instance, go to a newsstand and pick up a copy of Globus or pick up a copy of Slobacna Dalmacija, just as they would today? Yesterday, you said these were times of publication that people in Sarajevo and Mostar and other places would also pick up and read, even if it was not the a local press; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that following on this same theme, Ms. Alaburic also asked you about something to the effect of, Was it true that only about 10 per cent of people in the former Yugoslavia might get their news from newspapers or printed media, as opposed to more, I suppose, like many people in many countries I think today, for better or for worse, getting much of their information from the electronic media. And I don't think there was any specific firm information on that, but let's assume, for the moment, that if it's something like 10 or 25 per cent of the population looks at newspapers. Now, if that's the case can you tell us among that 10 or 25 per cent, what percentage of people in that percentage of people where do you think the more educated people in any given culture or society would fall? Within that 10 or 25 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I think before this question is put, we have to establish whether this witness is a population expert. He cannot answer this question as a historian. He can answer it as an average person who is informed about the conditions and the situation in the former Yugoslavia if he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to clarify the following. I think it is not correct to put a question ranging from 10 to 25 per cent, because if it refers to my question, the figure I gave was 10 per cent, and this is a result of research carried out at the time. It refers to the consumption of the entire press, which included women's magazines, motoring magazines, and so on and so forth. So the percentage of the population who read political weeklies and newspapers was exceptionally small. This can also be concluded from the circulation of Danas and Vreme at the time, which was about 25.000 for Danas in mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Danas--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please remain seated. What Mrs. Alaburic stated was very clear. She said she spoke of 10 per cent and not 25 per cent, so let's stay with 10 per cent. Mr. Kovacic raised an objection with regard to the skills of the witness or his ability to discuss statistics. Mr. Miller, what do you have to say on that topic? One of the Defence counsels feels that you are not able, on the basis of a figure, a statistical figure, to give an appropriate answer. What could you answer? And then my colleague would also like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say the following: It is already high time to let Mr. Scott finish his examination -- re-examination, and, really, I would like to ask the teams of the Defence to let him to do that. You are six teams. If you continue this way, to speak about a minor question, in my view, it is a very minor question, how many percentage of a country is reading this or that newspaper, and now you are taking this time away from the Prosecution. So I would like to ask Mr. Miller to answer Judge Antonetti's question, and to let afterwards to let Mr. Scott to finish with his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before that, Your Honour, I would, again, Your Honour, I would like to be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to be heard to respond to the Defence before we go to the next question of the witness. Let me have a response to what the Defence says before the Court goes further. What we've seen here is, once again, the same thing that what Mr. Karnavas was objecting to earlier. There is one set of rules for the Defence and one set of rules for the Prosecution. It was okay, it was okay, yesterday, for Ms. Alaburic to assert facts which is not evidence. She is not testifying, but she says, "I think it's 10 per cent." That's not evidence. There is no evidence in the record that says that. It's Ms. Alaburic's suggestion. She may have researched it, that's fine. I can go and conducts my research as well. There is no evidence in the record that it's 10 per cent. We have -- with all due respect to Ms. Alaburic, it's not evidence. Now, all I'm simply putting to the witness is -- and, further, when she asked him that question, and, again, as did Mr. Karnavas, when she got an answer from the witness, she didn't object, Well, the witness doesn't have any basis to answer that. So now I'm following up, trying to clarify, and I get an objection. It's just not fair, Your Honour. This is absolutely unfair the way these objections are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Mr. Scott. Nonetheless, yes, I agree that you are right. But Mr. Miller, with regard to statistics, can you give an answer? Yesterday, apparently you were, so what about today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was. I think I just went with what was suggested to me. I have no special training on the demography of Croatian or the readership of these journals. I spent a lot of time studying, especially in the Serbian context, in modern politics, and I don't think there has been a whole lot of research that would actually establish the sorts of answers that we are looking for here. Yesterday, when the question was put to me, it was stated that 10 per cent -- actually, the question got garbled, you might remember, in the translation in the transcription. At first, it said one thing; and, then, I believe, in the second instance, it said 10 per cent used the print media and 90 per cent use the electronic media. There was no electronic media, unless I'm not understanding the concept properly, in 1991 and 1992. I would suggest that, just as sort of generally, intuitively even, that 10 per cent, if it's true today, would have been much higher in 1991. But, no, I don't have any special training on this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, yes, indeed, I did note yesterday that there was some confusion. You mentioned electronic media. I thought perhaps you were referring to television and radio. Is that what you meant? You weren't referring to internet because in 1991, well, that didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the electronic media is a term covering primarily radio and television. In the early 1990s, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, there were republican radio and television stations. There were several in each republican centre, and each regional centre had its own radio station. In the early 1990s, private radio and TV stations began to be established on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, so that there were also radio and television stations at municipal level. Any serious investigation of public opinion or what can be considered to be common knowledge in that certain area could certainly not bypass the electronic media. This was what my question referred to, in essence: That one cannot conclude about the state of common knowledge based exclusively on the printed media, especially those which had very small circulations on their own markets and were not sold at all on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just as a footnote, let me refer to footnote 8, where, in fact, Radio Zagreb was quoted. It would not be correct to say that the witness did not at all take cognizance of electronic media. I have another little problem, Mr. Miller. I see a certain contradiction in what you said yesterday and today about the selection of these two weeklies. Today, you have said, and this is on page 30, line 16, 17, that you picked these because you thought they were representative, representative of broader coverage. Yesterday, you find that on page 85, on line 17, you said that you picked these because they were reliable. And, in my view, these are two different things. Representative and reliable is not the same. Very often, things that are popular and less serious may be more reliable for the general opinion. I would like to you comment on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine. I would happy to. I was adopting the word "representative" from Mr. Scott's question; and in his question, I believe he said, he acknowledged that I had already argued that much -- that this was much more moderate coverage than some of the material I did not include. And so what I meant today by "representative" was that this was sort of a standard basic understanding that we can assume on the part of the population of former Yugoslavia. I did choose -- I mean my approach might not have been the type of approach that lends itself to legal analysis, I don't know, but my own approach as a historian was to take evidence from those journals that I found to be and that I believe would be acknowledged to be most reliable. I don't -- it's sort of -- these are addressing two different questions about the way I framed my research. Does that explain it? I mean, I don't feel a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, as Judge Prandler said, we really need to move to what is essential. I completely share his points of view. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can just finish up on Judge Trechsel's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say -- let me go back to what you just said, Dr. Miller. Can I put it this way in terms of when you say reliable and representative: When you say it was "reliable" -- I guess my question that flows from that is: When you say it was "reliable," was it uniquely these two articles that were the only sources reporting this type of information or similar information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. As I said before, the others were reporting it perhaps even more loudly, more prominently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, going back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I regret to the Chamber that it's taken us this long; although, I think, I'm looking to Ms. Winter and my actual time is quite a small fraction that's been used in terms of the time on the clock. So I am trying to move as quickly as I can, without the interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to the point by -- that Ms. Alaburic was attempting to make or was making and putting fair questions to you about this, and that's why we got off on this, whether it was 10 per cent or something more. But to avoid any further argument, let's say 10 per cent. It's not in the record, there is no evidence, but let's just assume 10 per cent. Would you, basically, as a historian, as an educated person yourself, would you -- can you inform the Chamber of your view as to whether 10 per cent of the population that would read the print media, so to speak, would typically include the more educated members of that particular culture or society: People were university educations, people that were trained in business, people that have government positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That would include, for example, professional soldiers with a military academy education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: An assistant Minister of Defence in Croatia with an extensive university education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A trained economist, economics professor, and a local and regional politician who was president of a self-declared regional government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A defence department or ministry head with a university degree in economics and previously an assistant Minister of Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The head of a military police with an engineering degree and who had been the director of -- a director of a significant mining business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at the bundle that has been marked as Exhibit P10285?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in light of the challenges that were made to your second report about Herceg-Bosna, and in terms of the -- some of the comments about Herceg-Bosna, or a third entity being illegal or unconstitutional, I would just like to points to you several places in this bundle of documents which I've given you, which is again P10285. The first of these is a report on -- from the Peace Implementation Conference in December 1996. And if I can please direct your attention, for example, to page 5 of that document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the paragraph numbered 9, just, again, as we lead into this topic: "The Peace Implementation Council reaffirms that all administrative and other structures in the Federation must now be fully and irreversibly integrated and calls for the immediate dissolution or where appropriate transfer to the Federation of remaining structures of the so-called Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna or the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which are not in accordance with the constitution." If I can ask you then to go to the page 20 -- excuse me, page 8 of that same document, if I'm not -- no, I'm sorry. My apology. If you go to the next document, which would be on page 16 of the bundle -- let me make sure. I apologise. At page 16 of the bundle, there is a document titled, "The 9th Report of the High Representative for implementation of the Bosnian Peace Agreement." This is a report in April of 1998. And if I can ask you to go to page 8 of the report itself, which is page 23 in e-court, but page 8 of that particular report, number 53, paragraph 53: "There is still evidence that structures of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the 'Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna' continued to operate, despite the fact that they should have been disbanded following the establishment of Federation structures and common institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My office," that is the office of the High Representative, "will continue its efforts to disband these parallel structures." If I can ask to you go to the next document in the bundle, which is at e-court page 31, it is an article by the High Representative, dated February 12 of 2001. It's an article by the High Representative entitled, "Jelavic and HDZ play on the card of fear and work against Croats." And on the page 2 of that -- of that article, on page 32 in e-court, there is a paragraph that is titled, "There will be no third entity": "It is also clear that there will be no third entity. The cap badges are nothing more than a blue print for a territory doomed to poverty and isolation. Any self-proclaimed third entity would be sealed and sanctioned by the international community." And, then, it goes on to point out again, as we've heard before, how such an entity would, in fact, exclude Croats in other parts of Bosnia. If I can ask you to go to the next document in the bundling which, is the decision of the High Representative, dated March 7, 2001, which is page 34 in e-court. This is the "Official Decision of the High Representative." And going to the second page of his decision, on page 35 in e-court, second paragraph on that page, reads: "Instead, Mr. Jelavic has directed violated the constitutional order of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This culminated on Saturday, 3 March, 2001 in Mostar, with the unconstitutional initiative led by Mr. Ante Jelavic, to undermine the constitutional order of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Bosnia-Herzegovina and establish an illegal parallel structure." And, at the bottom of that page, when he's talking about these efforts, at the very last line on this page: "on the establishment of an unconstitutional and illegal parallel structure. The top of the following page, page 36 in e-court, the High Representative refers in that paragraph to "illegal or anti-Dayton activities including the establishment and maintenance of parallel structures." In his first paragraph, under "Conclusions," he refers to the "illegal initiative." Now, sir, in the interests of time, since we've already gone quite long, these documents, would that be further support and consistent with what you say in your report about the -- you were taken to task for using at one point the word "illegal structures." Does this support your report in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, specifically, another document, which is in the third binder which was exhibited before, but we didn't get to it specifically, was P10284. I cite that one in particular because that is specifically cited at footnote 23 of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P10284 is the 19th Report by the High Representative to the Secretary-General of the United Nations covering the periods from February to June 2001. At the bottom of the page, under 1 and then bullet item: "On the third of March, the HDZ, which had been ousted from power by the alliance for changes after the November elections, proclaimed the so-called Croat self-rule. Four days later I decided to remove Mr. Jelavic, the Croat member of the BiH Presidency and HDZ president from his positions, as he personally led this serious violation of the constitutional order. On the 6th of April, I appointed a provisional administrator for the Hercegovacka Banka, which acted as the financial backbone of the HDZ-led illegal parallel structures." On page 4 of that same report, paragraph number 10, the High Representative gives a further account of these efforts. And just in light of the other issues about the separate army, at the end of paragraph number 10, and as cited in your report, specifically cited in your report, that is the event: "On the 13 March, HDZ officials ordered the disbanding of the Croat components of the Federation army, followed on 28 March by a walkout of Croat officers and soldiers from their barracks." Paragraph 11: "The efforts of this illegal 'Croat self-ruled' control the Federation financial institutions, mainly the customs office, and the Croat majority areas has failed thanks to the firm attitude of the federation government." You can confirm to me, I'm sure, that this report is cited at footnote 23 of your Herceg-Bosna report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, finally, the last document in the big bundle that is in the last bundle we were looking at, which is P10285. The bundle of documents we were just looking at. If you can turn to the last document, which is a press release from the office of the High Representative, dated the 23rd of March 2001: "UN Security Council supports High Representative, condemns attempt to establish Croat self-rule in BiH. At its meeting yesterday in New York, the United Nations Security Council condemned 'recent unilateral moves by the so-called Croat National Congress to establish Croat self-rule in open contradictions of the provisions of the peace agreement.'" And, then, that goes on to the second to last paragraph, on that page: "The action taken by the High Representative fully endorsed and supported by the EU which," at the end of that paragraph, "condemns the unilateral moves by the so-called Croat National Congress to place themselves outside the provisions of the Dayton peace accords." Next page: Fully applauded and approved by the US representative Mark Minton. Next paragraph: Fully endorsed and supported by the French representative to the Security Council, and so on. Sir, do those additional documents I've shown you support your report and the conclusions stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the gentleman be asked by the Bench where in these documents does it show that at least my client, Dr. Prlic, was involved in any of these events. I'd also ask the gentleman, since he read the indictment, where is Mr. Jelavic in the indictment and to what extent his activities in 2001 have anything to do with this particular trial. This is the whole point. Why is this relevant? I sat there. I've allowed him to go on. He's made his record. But the bottom line is, we need to know why is this relevant considering the time and scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, these aren't questions for the witness. They are arguments by counsel. The Chamber already ruled, originally, in accepting this person's testimony and the report -- to receive the reports, at least provisionally, and indicating that it was relevant. And for the very same reasons they were relevant at that time, they remain relevant. As to the particular individual involvement of various persons in these efforts, if various parties want to go into that, it certainly may come up again in the future, but it was not, again, not the intended scope of this witness. But the witness was challenged, was specifically challenged, on his second report and especially on the characterisation of these efforts, these entities being illegal. And the evidence is clearly, in my view, I'm arguing, I'm counsel, I submit that the evidence is consistent with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I don't usually participate a great deal in all this. I'm not a lawyer, of course; although, I was a professor at the Faculty of Law before my indictment. As this is redirect, two points were put, two theses were put. Yesterday, my counsel asked whether the taking over of functions by Herceg-Bosna and the establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Federation, was a parallel process, and these documents speak to that. The international community is asking for these functions to be transferred, both from Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second issue that was raised was one of illegality. The title of the document is, "The Persistence of Herceg-Bosna." So the fact that it lasted and the illegality of the constitutional -- of the institutions in the documents presented here, we are dealing with decisions made in 2001. In both these decisions and the comments from the office of the High Representative, and the UN documents, it says that illegal structures were created, establishment, the establishment of illegal structures. So these are illegal structures created in 2001. In my view, the duty of all of us in this courtroom is to put our case correctly. That's why I wanted to raise these two issues; although, this type of redirect calls for new examination by the Defence, in view of the types of questions put, because points that were raised very clearly during the cross-examination were now put in a quite different context, both as regards their contents and their time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, with Your Honour's leave put, one question to the witness? He said that he read Hrvatski Vojnik, and that publication was published by an institution I worked in. It was -- I was one of the founders. So does the witness know what kind of texts and viewpoints were expressed in that publication? And, secondly, certain political stand points are being transformed here into legal acts, legal documents. The stand points of the High Representative on self-administration which have changed today are supposed to produce criminal activity regardless of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it so happens that you [as interpreted] are one of the founders of the publication you have read, so he's asking you whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. In the transcript, it is not "you," but "Mr. Praljak." It says that, "you are one of the founders." No. Mr. Praljak is one of the founders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's exactly what I said. Mr. Praljak was one of the founders of this magazine. Were you aware of that? And he's asking you what was the purpose of this magazine? What kind of ideas did it convey? These are the kind of thing he would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, and you might recall that I wasn't even entirely certain of the title, I was including it in a long list of magazines that I occasionally read back in the early 1990s. It's been that long since I looked at it, and I really couldn't characterise the content in any kind of depth or breadth at this point. It is interesting to find out, which I did not know, that Mr. Praljak was a founder of that magazine. If and when I read it in the future, that will perhaps make it even more interesting than it would normally be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions and I thank the Chamber for the time that was allowed, and thank you, Dr. Miller.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
