utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't wish to interrupt my colleague, Mr. Scott, while he was asking questions about whether the various ministries were within that 10 per cent of the population that reads the papers. But I'd like to be allowed to ask one or two questions now, to ask the witness some questions, because I think the way in which this was formulated by Mr. Scott implies the existence of a Yugoslavia market for newspapers and the possibility that, in any place in the former Yugoslavia, any type of media could be accessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask, therefore, the witness the following question: Do you know that, as of the autumn of 1991, some publications that were published in Belgrade were not accessible to citizens in Croatia, so the citizens of Croatia couldn't read these papers; as, indeed, the Ministry of Defence or the government, they could not read those publications either, Serbian publications, or rather, publications printed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And my next question, in view of the fact that we are dealing with Bosnia-Herzegovina: Does the same situation apply to Bosnia-Herzegovina? What we said for Croatia, does it also apply to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did the same situation prevail there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only offer an educated guess. Would that be adequate?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, can we conclude that you cannot confirm the fact that, at the end of 1991 and during 1992, the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina was able to read Vreme, Danas, or any other Belgrade or Zagreb publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Zagreb in 1992, so I know that the media market had closed up. I can only say that since Bosnia was not actively involved in warfare during most of -- well, technically, all of 1991, that Sarajevo, I would guess, had access to both types of press, probably more likely to have Vreme than Danas, if we are going to use those two as examples. But, of course, I don't have any scientific knowledge on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's leave scientific knowledge for the time being. Do you have any other knowledge, other than your assumptions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mrs. Alaburic, may I ask you what kind of procedure this is. We've had direct, we've had cross, and we've had redirect. What you are raising you could have raised in cross. What is the justification for prolonging this morning by raising these again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not able to ask these questions during the cross-examination because this particular matter was raised only in redirect, re-examination. And I think that Mr. Scott, on the basis of the questions I asked during my cross-examination, tried to say that the Ministry of Defence and the authorities generally were able to access and read Vreme and Danas, and that that was somebody creating a certain policy and then could reap knowledge from Danas and Vreme as a source. So I thought that this would mislead the Trial Chamber, and my exclusive intention was to assist the Trial Chamber in understanding the fact that a Yugoslav market did not exist, and that's why I thought it relevant to ask these additional questions. I refrained from objecting when Mr. Scott was asking these while he was asking them. Now, if you consider that to be improper, next time, every time, I will rise to my feet and utter my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to make an objection with respect to the proceedings, the process. I think it is with critical value, relative critical value. I can do this without the presence of the witness, but may I have three minutes to raise my objection on procedure, procedural matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am referring to the undoubtable rights of the accused given by the Statute and Rules and Regulations of this Tribunal to be precisely informed about the accusations and counts they -- that stand before them. We heard through this testimony and the expert report, at least with respect to the post-Dayton Accord report, that the Prosecution was quite frank and open, saying that they would wish to prove their thesis about the extension of the HR HB after Dayton as well. So that's quite clear. On the other hand, when we look at the indictment, especially paragraphs 15 and 16, we have defined the time for the duration of this famous HZ HB as part of a joint criminal enterprise, and we are told in that portion or excerpt that that institution of the joint criminal enterprise, in which the HZ HB was the main instrument, that it lasted from the 18th of November until April 1994. We've just now heard, or rather, we have been discussing this for two days now, according to the second expert report, and also by the express statements of the person representing the OTP, it was precisely stated and quite clearly stated that through this evidence, they are maintaining that the HZ HB continued to exist. Ergo, I must understand this as a criminal enterprise, because that's how the indictment defines it, even after the Dayton agreement. Now we know according to practice at this Tribunal, and you'll remember what I'm talking about, that there were many, many problems with the murky way in which the -- and unclear way in which the indictment was compiled, and there was an appeals judgement. If I may rephrase it, it says, more or less, the following, that the accused could have been informed about changes in the indictment -- could be informed about changes in the indictment during the proceedings and the conduct of the Prosecution and the exhibits presented by the Prosecution during the proceedings. In other words, if the accused were sleeping during the proceedings going on, for example, and didn't understand that the Prosecution could, through its exhibits, in fact, change and amend the indictment, then that was to his detriment. Now, learning from that example and following case law and court practice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber must rule on a criminal enterprise that extends until April 1994, not beyond. If the Prosecution wishes to amend the indictment, the Prosecution must submit a motion. So there is no amendment to the indictment simply because Mr. Scott is addressing questions to the witness. So let me reassure you on this point. The Trial Chamber, when it rules, will not say that the criminal enterprise lasted until 1995, because within the scope of the indictment, there is a limit. It is April 1994. It does not go until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I wanted to hear, the position of the Trial Chamber. So, as the Trial Chamber, you have now given me instructions and guidelines, that I need not defend my clients for everything that happened after 1994; that is to say, after the Washington agreement or after the date stipulated in the indictment. That is your position as the Trial Chamber, and now I have received my answer and relevant information about what the indictment actually states and is. However, Your Honours, and this is my proposal, that you request of the Prosecution explicitly to state here whether the assertions that we have heard over the past two days here, referring to the second expert report, whether by that the Prosecutor is in effect modifying and amending the indictment, because it is the right of the Prosecution to amend the indictment or modify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, on this legal issue, what is your opinion? I think -- I think I've understood now that Mr. Kovacic would like to know your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour the short answer - and I would be happy to discuss that at greater length when the time allows and, I think, when the witness has been excused. I really don't see any reason to have the witness here for this - but we are not seeking to amend the indictment. But this evidence, in our view, is directly relevant to the time charged in the indictments and to issues raised in the indictment. And, again, I'd be happy to get into that at another time without the witness and with certain things that are in closed session. As to why these are relevant, the short answer is we are not amending the indictment. But to be very clear, it's the Prosecution position is the evidence that's been given in the last several days is extremely relevant to what is charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for enabling us to get that reply. So now I'm quite certain that I need not put up a defence in relation to that. Now, my next proposal is that the Trial Chamber excludes this testimony and excludes both the expert reports because we've just heard that it's irrelevant -- or rather, to exclude the second expert report - I made a mistake - and part of the testimony referring to the second expert report because we just heard that it is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should take place in the following manner: The Prosecution will draw up a list of exhibits to be tendered with IC numbers. You will make your own list, state your objections, and this will be debated by the Trial Chamber. We shall not go into this debate now. It will take place before the Chamber, and the Chamber will hand down a written ruling. Very well, Mr. Miller, I would like to thank you. Your testimony has now come to an end; and on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to extend to you all of my best wishes for your return home. As we will now take a break, if there are no other questions to be raised. Well, no, I see Mr. Scott has risen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I know you probably didn't want to see me on my feet again. It's not for anything, I hope, that I don't think would be controversial. I would like to address one matter, which again, I don't think will be difficult. But, I think, again, it would be appropriate for the witness to be excused first, and then I would like to have one minute of the Chamber's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, witness, if you can now leave the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Scott, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think the Prosecution, as a whole, and myself personally, would be remiss if I did not take the opportunity. I didn't take the time yesterday. I had asked Mr. Murphy if he indeed to be here today to be assured of that, but I would like to add my thoughts and appreciation to Mr. Murphy to join those that were expressed by the Chamber yesterday. It's been a pleasure to work with Mr. Murphy as an advocate. I think the Chamber has had the privilege to see a very fine and effective advocate at work in this courtroom, and I want to express my best wishes to him. I think that, if I the Chamber would allow me. In sometimes watching what I sometimes considered to be the Murphy-Karnavas good cop-bad cop, I don't think anyone but Mr. Murphy could possibly better serve as a good cop. And if he won't be offended if I say this, as one good cop to another good cop, I express my thanks and best wishes for the work he has done, and I should say best wishes for the future as he goes into his new work. Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful to Mr. Scott for those kind words, and I couldn't think of a better way of retiring from the police force than with those kind observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you very much. And next week, as you know, we have some witness schedule. So we will meet on Monday at 2.15. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of October, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.48 a.m.,
